Introduction
Enals are important building blocks in chemical synthesis and
continue to be vital substrates for the development of
organocatalysis.<sup>[1–2]</sup> However, despite the enormous synthetic
utility, very few catalytic methods are available for the γ-
functionalization of enals. The direct site-selective γ-functional-
ization of unmodified enals has been challenging.<sup>[3–7]</sup> So far, the
known approaches relies on the remote carbonyl-directed γ-
functionalization via the electron-rich dienyl motifs such as
Mukaiyama dienolsilylethers,<sup>[3]</sup> metal-dienolates<sup>[4]</sup> and dien-
amines (Scheme 1A).<sup>[5,6]</sup> However, these approaches often suffer
from the competitive α-functionalization and cycloaddition
pathways of the conformationally labile 4-carbon dienyl
motif.<sup>[5,8,9]</sup> Therefore, given the limitations associated with the
existing strategies, the development of general, efficient, and
operationally simple new catalytic approaches to the syntheti-
cally useful γ-functionalized enals would be highly valuable.
Metal carbenes derived from diazo compounds are valuable
reactive intermediates that are central to a wide range of
carbene transfer reactions such as σ-bond insertions (C�H, C�X,
and X�H; X = heteroatom), cycloadditions, and ylide rearrange-
ment reactions.<sup>[10,11]</sup> In particular, the ability of carbenoids to
offer geminal difunctionalization through acceptor/donor reac-
tivity provides rapid molecular complexity. Inspired by the
petitive side reactions. The synthetic utility of the γ-
allenyl(sulfanyl)enals was demonstrated by the InCl -catalyzed
cycloisomerization to the trisubstituted furanyl-enals via an
unusual 1,4-sulfanyl migration. In addition, an operationally
simple and efficient one-pot [3+ 2] annulation of diazoenals
and propargyl sulfides, involving combined γ-difunctionaliza-
tion and cycloisomerization was successfully developed for the
diverse enal-functionalized furans.

Results and Discussion
In continuation of our ongoing studies on the synthetic
applications of diazoenals,<sup>[12–15]</sup> we recently reported the site-
selective γ-amination via enalcarbenoid NH-insertion reaction
with propargyl amine. The resulting donor-acceptor dienamine
intermediates were successfully utilized in the construction of
valuable enal-functionalized 1,4-oxazine heterocycles.<sup>[13]</sup> In-
spired by these studies, we next examined the carbene transfer
reaction of diazoenal 1 a and phenyl propargyl sulfide 2 a
anticipating C�S & C�C bond forming direct γ-difunctionaliza-
tion through the sulfur ylide [2,3] sigmatropic rearrangement.<sup>[16]</sup>
Gratifyingly, a variety of dirhodium carboxylates such as
Rh (OAc) , Rh (oct) , Rh (tfa) and Rh (esp) efficiently catalyzed
the reaction producing γ-quaternized γ-allenyl(sulfanyl)enal 3
in 85–95 % yield (Table 1, entries 1–4). The bulky chiral Rh {(S)-
DOSP} required longer reaction time and gave allene 3 in
reduced yield (65%) with the marginal enantioselectivity (5 %
ee). The best yield was obtained with 1 mol % Rh (OAc) at
ambient conditions (95 %, entry 1). The reaction was compatible
with other halogenated solvents, and toluene, whereas oxy-
genated solvents are not compatible (See SI for full optimiza-
tion table).

To understand the mechanism of the furan formation, a
series of control experiments were carried out (Scheme 2). A
1: 1 mixture of allene 7 and 15 was subjected to the rearrange-
ment reaction in the presence of 3 mol % InCl . Interestingly, in
addition to the anticipated furans 36 and 43, the reaction also
produced considerable amounts of crossed furan products 44
and 32 through intermolecular sulfide migration (Scheme 2A).
Performing the cycloisomerization of allene 7 in the presence of
4-methylthiophenol 66 produced furan 36 along with the
crossed furan 44 in about a 2 : 1 ratio (Scheme 2B). Further, a
large-scale cycloisomerization reaction of 7 led to the detection
of a trace amount of diphenyl disulfide 67 (Scheme 2C).
However, treating furan 36 with 4-methylthiophenol 66 in the
presence of InCl failed to produce the crossed furan 44
(Scheme 2D), indicating that sulfanyl migration is irreversible.
Based on the control experiments, a plausible mechanism
for the [3 + 2] annulation via γ-difunctionalization and cyclo-

The synthetic utility of the furanyl-enal 35 was demon-
strated by further transformations (Scheme 4). Chemoselective
oxidation using m-CPBA, gave a mixture of sulfone 74 and
sulfoxide 75 in 76 % and 22 % yield respectively.<sup>[22]</sup>. The
structure of 74 has been confirmed by the single crystal X-ray
diffraction. Olefination of furanyl-enal 35 with phosphorane 76
produced the valuable dienone-tethered furan 77 in 81 % yield.

To understand the mechanism of the furan formation, a
series of control experiments were carried out (Scheme 2). A
1: 1 mixture of allene 7 and 15 was subjected to the rearrange-
ment reaction in the presence of 3 mol % InCl . Interestingly, in
addition to the anticipated furans 36 and 43, the reaction also
produced considerable amounts of crossed furan products 44
and 32 through intermolecular sulfide migration (Scheme 2A).
Performing the cycloisomerization of allene 7 in the presence of
4-methylthiophenol 66 produced furan 36 along with the
crossed furan 44 in about a 2 : 1 ratio (Scheme 2B). Further, a
large-scale cycloisomerization reaction of 7 led to the detection
of a trace amount of diphenyl disulfide 67 (Scheme 2C).
However, treating furan 36 with 4-methylthiophenol 66 in the
presence of InCl failed to produce the crossed furan 44
(Scheme 2D), indicating that sulfanyl migration is irreversible.
Based on the control experiments, a plausible mechanism
for the [3 + 2] annulation via γ-difunctionalization and cyclo-
isomerization reaction, involving Rh(II) and In(III) catalytic cycles
is depicted in Scheme 3. The Rh-enalcarbenoid 68 derived from
diazoenal 1 reacts with propargyl sulfide 2 to give sulfonium
ylide 69A. Subsequent [2,3] sigmatropic rearrangement of 69A
or the metal-free ylide 69 B leads to the γ-allenyl(sulfanyl)enal
70. The low enantioselectivity
observed for Table 1,
entry 5 may support the metal free ylide rearrangement. In the
In-catalysis, intramolecular allylic sulfide displacement via 5-
endo-dig heterocyclization of In(III) activated allenyl sulfide 71
results in the unstable 2-methylene-2H-furan-1-ium and Indium-
thiolate ion pair 72. The involvement of this ion pair
intermediate supports the results of the control experiments
(Scheme 2). Finally, the recombination of ion pair 72 by the
thiolate nucleophilic addition completes the 1,4-sulfanyl
migration<sup>[21]</sup> and furnishes the enal-functionalized furan product

The synthetic utility of the furanyl-enal 35 was demon-
strated by further transformations (Scheme 4). Chemoselective
oxidation using m-CPBA, gave a mixture of sulfone 74 and
sulfoxide 75 in 76 % and 22 % yield respectively.<sup>[22]</sup>. The
structure of 74 has been confirmed by the single crystal X-ray
diffraction. Olefination of furanyl-enal 35 with phosphorane 76
produced the valuable dienone-tethered furan 77 in 81 % yield.
Conclusions
In summary, we have developed a new approach for the
synthetically important γ-difunctionalized enals. The strategy
involves rhodium-catalyzed direct
\mathsf { C } \mathrm { - } \mathsf { C } \ \& \ \mathsf { C } \mathrm { - } \mathsf { S }
bond forming
site-selective γ-difunctionalization of diazoenals with aryl prop-
argyl sulfides via sulfur ylide [2,3] sigmatropic rearrangement
and provides functionally rich γ-allenyl(sulfanyl)enals in excel-
lent yield at ambient temperature. The synthetic utility of the
new enals was demonstrated by the InCl -catalyzed cyclo-
isomerization to the trisubstituted furanyl-enals via an unusual
1,4-sulfanyl migration. Moreover, an operationally simple and
efficient one-opt [3 + 2] annulation of diazoenals and aryl
propargyl sulfides gave diverse enal-functionalized furans.
Further study on the synthetic applications of γ-difinctionaliza-
tion and [3+2] annulation is ongoing.
